title: Threads & executors
scopeHtml: Thread lifecycle, interrupts, ExecutorService types, ThreadPoolExecutor internals, queues and rejection, pool sizing, ForkJoinPool and parallel streams, scheduled executors, ThreadLocal in pools, graceful shutdown, naming and monitoring. (Virtual threads, locks, CompletableFuture and deadlocks are owned by other chunks.)

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the states a Java thread goes through. What is the difference between BLOCKED and WAITING, and does RUNNABLE mean the thread is on a CPU?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Thread dumps are the first tool in any concurrency incident. If you cannot read the states precisely, you misdiagnose.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Thread.State has six values: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED. BLOCKED means the thread is trying to enter a synchronized block or re-enter after wait() and another thread owns the monitor. WAITING means it called something like Object.wait(), join() or LockSupport.park() and needs another thread's action to wake it. TIMED_WAITING is the same with a timeout (sleep, wait(ms), parkNanos). RUNNABLE only means 'eligible to run in the JVM's view'. It may be on a CPU, queued for one, or sitting in a native blocking call like a socket read."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The JVM exposes states through Thread.getState() and the thread dump. They are JVM-level states, not OS scheduler states.

NEW --start()--> RUNNABLE <--------------------------+
                  |  |  |                             |
   monitor busy   |  |  | wait()/join()/park()        | notified / unparked / timeout
                  v  |  v                             |
              BLOCKED |  WAITING / TIMED_WAITING -----+
                      |
            run() ends / uncaught exception
                      v
                 TERMINATED
  • NEW: object constructed, start() not yet called. start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException.
  • RUNNABLE: includes running on CPU, runnable but waiting for a core, and executing a native method. A thread blocked in SocketInputStream.read shows RUNNABLE because the JVM does not know the OS has parked it. This is why a thread dump full of RUNNABLE threads in socketRead0 is an IO wait, not CPU burn.
  • BLOCKED: only for intrinsic monitors (synchronized). Waiting on a ReentrantLock is not BLOCKED; it parks, so it shows WAITING (parking) with the lock's AQS frames.
  • WAITING: indefinite. Object.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park() (used by ReentrantLock, Condition, Future.get, BlockingQueue.take).
  • TIMED_WAITING: sleep, wait(timeout), join(timeout), parkNanos, poll(timeout).
  • TERMINATED: run() returned or threw. A Thread object cannot be restarted.

Reading a dump: many threads BLOCKED on the same monitor address (waiting to lock <0x...>) is monitor contention. Many WAITING in LinkedBlockingQueue.take are just idle pool workers. Many RUNNABLE in the same native read frame is IO latency from a dependency.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
    synchronized (LOCK) { /* ... */ }
});
System.out.println(t.getState()); // NEW
t.start();                        // RUNNABLE (soon BLOCKED if LOCK is held)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying RUNNABLE means "using CPU". Cross-check with top -H or async-profiler CPU mode.
  • Believing lock waits on ReentrantLock appear as BLOCKED. They appear as WAITING/TIMED_WAITING in Unsafe.park.
  • Thinking you can call start() again after TERMINATED.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you tell CPU-bound RUNNABLE from IO-bound RUNNABLE in a dump? → Look at the top frame: socketRead0, epollWait, FileInputStream.readBytes are IO; application/hash/regex frames are CPU. Confirm with top -H -p <pid> (convert thread id to hex, match nid=0x..).
  2. What is a thread's state while it waits in ExecutorService.submit().get()? → WAITING (parked in FutureTask.awaitDone).
  3. Is BLOCKED ever caused by Object.wait()? → Yes, after being notified the thread must re-acquire the monitor; if it is held it moves WAITING -> BLOCKED, so a notified thread can show BLOCKED.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer lists the six states from memory. A senior ties them to evidence: reads a jstack dump, distinguishes monitor vs park-based waits, knows RUNNABLE hides native IO, and uses that to decide between a CPU profile and a dependency-latency investigation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams routinely "see 400 RUNNABLE threads" and assume CPU saturation when the box is at 15% CPU and every thread is in a socket read to a slow database.

questions.promptHtml: What is a daemon thread, when does the JVM exit, and why can daemon threads be dangerous for background work that must finish?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of JVM shutdown semantics and why services hang on exit or lose data.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread finishes (or System.exit is called). Daemon threads do not keep the JVM alive and are killed abruptly: no finally blocks, no cleanup. So a daemon thread is right for housekeeping you can lose, like a metrics flusher, and wrong for anything that must complete, like writing a file or committing an offset. Conversely, a leaked non-daemon pool thread will keep a process from exiting."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• setDaemon(true) must be called before start(), otherwise IllegalThreadStateException. A new thread inherits the daemon flag of the thread that creates it.
  • When the main method returns and only daemon threads remain, the JVM begins shutdown: runs shutdown hooks, then halts. Daemon threads simply stop mid-instruction. Any try/finally or try-with-resources in them does not run. Half-written files, unflushed buffers and unreleased locks (in other processes/DB sessions) follow.
  • Executors.defaultThreadFactory() creates non-daemon threads. That is why a forgotten newFixedThreadPool makes main return but the process never exits. ForkJoinPool.commonPool() threads are daemon, which is why a program whose only remaining work is a CompletableFuture.supplyAsync can exit before it finishes.
  • Virtual threads are always daemon (Java 21); see the virtual-thread chunk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
public static void main(String[] args) {
    Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
        try { Thread.sleep(5_000); System.out.println("done"); }
        finally { System.out.println("cleanup"); } // never printed if daemon
    });
    t.setDaemon(true);
    t.start();
    // main returns -> JVM exits immediately, "done" and "cleanup" are lost
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Making a pool daemon "so shutdown doesn't hang" instead of shutting it down properly; you then lose in-flight work on SIGTERM.
  • Calling setDaemon after start().
  • Forgetting that pool threads are non-daemon by default, so tests and CLI tools hang.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A batch job's main finishes but the process stays up. First thing you check? → jstack for non-daemon threads ("..." #12 prio=5 without daemon), almost always an un-shutdown executor or Timer.
  2. Does System.exit wait for non-daemon threads? → No. It runs shutdown hooks and halts regardless.
  3. How do you make a daemon-based pool and still not lose work on exit? → Register a shutdown hook (or framework lifecycle) that calls shutdown() + awaitTermination; a daemon flag alone gives no completion guarantee.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "daemon threads run in background, JVM does not wait for them." Senior: explains no finally, inheritance of the flag, default factory is non-daemon, common pool is daemon, and designs the shutdown path instead of using the flag as a shortcut.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scheduled-report service marked its writer pool daemon to fix slow redeploys; on each deploy half-written files were left behind.

questions.promptHtml: How does thread interruption work in Java? What do interrupt(), isInterrupted() and Thread.interrupted() do, and what should you do when you catch InterruptedException?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cooperative cancellation is the foundation for shutdown and timeouts. Swallowing interrupts is a classic senior-level code review catch.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "interrupt() does not stop a thread. It sets the thread's interrupt flag. Blocking methods like sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take check it, throw InterruptedException and clear the flag. isInterrupted() reads the flag without clearing it; static Thread.interrupted() reads and clears it. When I catch InterruptedException I either propagate it, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and exit promptly. I never swallow it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Interruption is a cooperative protocol. A request is stored as a boolean on the thread; the target decides what to do.

Situation Behaviour on interrupt()
In sleep/wait/join/take/poll(timeout) Wakes, throws InterruptedException, flag cleared
Flag set, then calls a blocking method Throws immediately
Running CPU loop Nothing, unless it polls isInterrupted()
ReentrantLock.lock() Not interruptible (use lockInterruptibly or tryLock(timeout))
synchronized entry Not interruptible
Blocking java.io stream/socket read Not interrupted; close the stream/socket from another thread
java.nio InterruptibleChannel Channel is closed, thread gets ClosedByInterruptException

Why restore the flag: the flag is the only signal. If you catch the exception and do nothing, callers higher up (a pool worker loop, shutdownNow) never learn they were asked to stop. If you cannot rethrow (e.g. in Runnable.run), re-set it.

ThreadPoolExecutor.shutdownNow() and Future.cancel(true) rely on exactly this: they interrupt the worker thread. A task that swallows interrupts survives them.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Correct
void run() {
    try {
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            Job j = queue.take();       // throws on interrupt
            process(j);
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore, then exit
    }
}

// Broken: swallowed, the pool can never stop this worker
catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted"); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (InterruptedException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } then keep looping.
  • Using Thread.interrupted() in a loop condition without realising it clears the flag.
  • Assuming interrupt() aborts a blocking JDBC/socket call.
  • Using deprecated Thread.stop() (terminally deprecated; throws UnsupportedOperationException since Java 20).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the exception clear the flag? → The exception already delivers the signal; keeping the flag would make the very next blocking call throw again, so the handler could not clean up with blocking calls. That is also why you must re-set it if you want the signal to continue.
  2. How do you cancel a task blocked on a socket read? → Close the socket (or use a read timeout/NIO); interrupt alone does nothing for classic blocking IO.
  3. A task ignores interrupts and shutdownNow() never finishes. What do you do? → Find it with jstack; fix the task to poll/propagate; as a last resort bound the wait and let the process exit via the orchestrator. Do not use Thread.stop.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "interrupt stops the thread" or "catch and log". Senior: cooperative protocol, flag clearing semantics, which blocking primitives honour it, restore-or-propagate rule, and links it to shutdownNow and Future.cancel(true).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A consumer loop that logged and swallowed InterruptedException made every deploy take the full 30s grace period before being SIGKILLed, leaving uncommitted offsets.

questions.promptHtml: Describe what Executors.newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool, newSingleThreadExecutor, newScheduledThreadPool and newWorkStealingPool actually build. Which of them would you avoid in production and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates know the names but not the queue and bound underneath, which is where OOMs come from.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "They are factory methods over ThreadPoolExecutor (or ForkJoinPool). Fixed uses core = max = n with an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so a slow consumer means unbounded memory growth. Cached uses core 0, max Integer.MAX_VALUE, a SynchronousQueue and 60s keep-alive, so a burst means unbounded thread creation. Single is fixed with n = 1 wrapped so you cannot reconfigure it. Scheduled uses a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor with an unbounded delay queue. Work-stealing is a ForkJoinPool. In production I construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly with a bounded queue, a named thread factory and an explicit rejection policy."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Factory Core / Max Queue Hidden risk
newFixedThreadPool(n) n / n LinkedBlockingQueue (capacity Integer.MAX_VALUE) Queue grows until OOM; latency grows silently
newCachedThreadPool() 0 / Integer.MAX_VALUE, 60s SynchronousQueue Thread explosion (each ~1 MB stack reserve) -> unable to create native thread
newSingleThreadExecutor() 1 / 1 unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue Same queue risk; result is wrapped (not a ThreadPoolExecutor you can cast)
newScheduledThreadPool(n) n / Integer.MAX_VALUE (max ignored) DelayedWorkQueue (unbounded) Accumulating tasks; never exceeds core
newWorkStealingPool() parallelism = availableProcessors() per-worker deques Not suited to blocking tasks; daemon threads
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() (21) thread per task none Unbounded concurrency; bound with a Semaphore. Covered in the virtual-thread chunk

The ThreadPoolExecutor javadoc itself states the queueing strategy trade-offs: direct hand-off (SynchronousQueue) needs an unbounded max; an unbounded queue means maximumPoolSize has no effect; a bounded queue guards resources but needs tuning.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 32, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),
    new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("orders-%d").build(), // Guava
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixed pool is safe because the thread count is bounded"; the queue is the unbounded part.
  • Using the cached pool for work that blocks on a slow dependency: threads pile up as latency rises.
  • Using Executors.newFixedThreadPool in a @Bean with no name, so thread dumps show pool-3-thread-7.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the cached pool OK for many short non-blocking tasks? → Idle threads are reused and die after 60s; the thread count tracks concurrent demand. The danger is only with slow/blocking or bursty work.
  2. Can you resize newSingleThreadExecutor? → No, it's wrapped in a delegating executor; use new ThreadPoolExecutor(1,1,...) if you need control.
  3. What does the Alibaba-style lint rule "forbid Executors.*" buy you? → It forces every pool to declare its queue bound, rejection policy and thread names at the construction site, which is where reviews catch overload behaviour.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists the pools and their use cases. Senior: names the queue and bound under each, predicts the failure mode (OOM vs thread explosion), and standardises on explicit ThreadPoolExecutor construction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Tens of services have been taken down by a newFixedThreadPool whose downstream slowed; the queue held millions of request objects until the heap filled.

questions.promptHtml: Explain exactly what ThreadPoolExecutor does when you call execute(task). What are corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, the queue and keepAlive, and why does a pool with a large queue never grow past core?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The core/queue/max ordering surprises most people. Getting it right shows you can predict behavior under load rather than hope.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "On execute: if fewer than core threads exist, start a new thread for this task even if others are idle. Otherwise try to offer the task to the queue. If the queue accepts it, done. If the queue is full, try to start a non-core thread up to max. If that also fails, call the RejectedExecutionHandler. So threads above core are only created when the queue is full. With an unbounded queue the queue never fills, so max is ignored."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
execute(task)
   |
   +-- workers < core ? --yes--> addWorker(task)   (new thread runs task first)
   |
   +-- queue.offer(task) ok ? --yes--> (re-check state; if 0 workers, add one)
   |
   +-- workers < max ? --yes--> addWorker(task)    (non-core thread)
   |
   +-- else --> handler.rejectedExecution(task, this)

Internals (OpenJDK ThreadPoolExecutor):

  • State and worker count are packed into one AtomicInteger ctl (top 3 bits run state: RUNNING, SHUTDOWN, STOP, TIDYING, TERMINATED; low 29 bits worker count). That is why the max pool size is capped near 2^29-1.
  • Each thread is a Worker (extends AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, implements Runnable) held in a HashSet guarded by mainLock. The Worker's non-reentrant lock lets the pool tell an idle worker (lock free, safe to interrupt on shutdown) from a busy one.
  • runWorker loops: run the first task if any, then getTask() repeatedly. getTask does queue.take() (core) or queue.poll(keepAlive) (when the worker is timeout-eligible). A worker returning null exits.
  • keepAlive applies to threads above core, or to all if allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true).
  • Core threads are created lazily on submission. prestartAllCoreThreads() starts them early.
  • If a task throws from execute(), the exception propagates to the worker, the worker thread dies (uncaught handler runs) and processWorkerExit replaces it. With submit() the exception is captured in the Future instead.
  • Edge: core = 0 with a queue; after enqueueing, the pool starts one worker so queued tasks are not stranded.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2));
// tasks 1,2 -> 2 core threads; tasks 3,4 -> queue; tasks 5,6 -> 2 extra threads (max 4)
// task 7 -> AbortPolicy -> RejectedExecutionException

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting max = 200 with new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() and expecting 200 threads.
  • Thinking tasks go to idle threads preferentially; a new core thread is spawned even if others are idle until core is reached.
  • Assuming order is preserved. Tasks submitted when the queue is full jump ahead of queued ones because new non-core threads run their task directly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you make the pool prefer extra threads over queueing? → Tomcat's TaskQueue trick: a custom queue whose offer returns false while pool size < max, forcing thread creation before queueing; or two pools chained through the rejection handler (the first with no queue). Say it is a hack and test it.
  2. What does allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) need? → keepAlive > 0, else IllegalArgumentException. Useful for bursty low-traffic pools.
  3. Why does the pool use ctl instead of a lock for state? → Lock-free fast path on execute; mainLock only guards the worker set and bookkeeping.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: recites core/max/queue. Senior: draws the three-step decision order, explains why unbounded queues neutralise max, mentions Worker/AQS and exception-kills-worker behavior, and knows the Tomcat-style override.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pool configured "core 10, max 100" never exceeded 10 threads because of an unbounded queue; latency climbed to 40s before anyone noticed, since no thread count ever changed.

questions.contextHtml:
An order-enrichment service runs on a pod with -Xmx1g, 2 vCPU. It calls a partner pricing API through Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20), submitting one task per incoming Kafka message (~800 msg/s). Normally each call takes 20 ms, so 20 threads handle 1000/s. At 14:02 the partner degrades to 250 ms per call (capacity now 20 / 0.25 = 80 calls/s). By 14:09 the pod restarts. Log before death: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space; GC logs show Full GCs every 2 s reclaiming nothing. CPU is 85% during GC. Consumer lag looked fine on the dashboard the whole time.

private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20);
void onMessage(Order o) { pool.submit(() -> enrich(o)); }
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened, how you would confirm it, and what you would change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap to 4 GB and add more threads." Memory is not the problem, the admission control is. More threads would hit the partner harder; bigger heap only delays the crash and lengthens the final GC.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the Kafka consumer acking before or after enrich completes (it sounds like before, which hides lag)? Is the partner call idempotent and does it have a timeout? What is the SLA on enrichment: can we drop or delay? Do other consumers share this pod's CPU?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart is a bandaid, so I would pause the consumer (or scale the partner-facing pool down via circuit breaker) and shed load: stop pulling new messages until the queue drains. If the partner is the issue, fail fast with a degraded path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue filled with tasks, each holding an Order and closure. (b) A memory leak in enrich. (c) Partner responses buffering. (d) GC mis-tuning. Evidence for (a): arrival 800/s minus service 80/s = 720 tasks/s accumulating; at ~1.5 KB per queued task that is about 1 MB/s, which would take ~15 minutes to fill 1 GB; at ~2.5 KB per task (order payload + lambda + FutureTask) it is 720 x 2.5 KB = 1.8 MB/s, roughly 7-9 minutes once live-set overhead is counted, which matches the timeline.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump on OOM (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError), open in Eclipse MAT, dominator tree: LinkedBlockingQueue$Node chain retaining millions of FutureTask. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram live shows the same. jstack would show all 20 workers in SocketInputStream.socketRead0. Micrometer queue-size gauge (absent today) would have shown the climb.
  5. Root cause: newFixedThreadPool has an unbounded queue; the submit path never pushes back; Kafka offsets were committed on submit, so the consumer saw no lag. Backlog lived in heap, invisible, until it exhausted it. Full GCs reclaimed nothing because the tasks were strongly reachable.
  6. Fix: Short term: bounded queue plus CallerRunsPolicy so the Kafka poll thread does the work itself and slows polling (natural backpressure), and a timeout on the partner call (e.g. 300 ms) with a circuit breaker. Long term: commit offsets after processing, limit in-flight with a Semaphore, and consider pausing the consumer when the pool's queue is above a high-water mark.
var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(20, 20, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
    namedFactory("enrich"),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
  1. Prevention: Alert on executor_queued_tasks and executor_queue_remaining; lint rule against Executors.newFixedThreadPool; load test with a slow stub (k6 + WireMock delay 250 ms) as a standard resilience test.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise heap or threads. CallerRunsPolicy stalls the poller and can exceed max.poll.interval.ms causing rebalances, so I'd instead pause/resume the consumer. Dropping with DiscardPolicy would silently lose orders.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the call is not idempotent and you commit after processing? → Use an idempotency key at the partner, or at-least-once with dedupe; never auto-retry blindly.
  • Queue size 200: how do you pick it? → In-flight budget = threads x tolerated wait. 200 tasks at 80/s is 2.5 s of backlog; sized for latency SLO, not memory.
  • What if CallerRunsPolicy triggers a Kafka rebalance? → Use consumer.pause() when queue passes 80% and resume() at 20%.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from several teams: dashboards showed healthy Kafka lag because offsets were committed at hand-off. The real backlog was a LinkedBlockingQueue 6 million deep. The postmortem action item was to alert on queue depth, not just lag.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only suggests more heap/threads; cannot explain why Full GC reclaims nothing.
  • Hire: Identifies unbounded queue, proposes bounded queue plus rejection policy and timeout.
  • Strong hire: Does the arrival-vs-service math, notes offset-commit masking, designs backpressure via pause/resume, and adds queue-depth alerting plus slow-dependency load test.

questions.promptHtml: What are the built-in RejectedExecutionHandler policies, when is each one acceptable, and what are the failure modes of CallerRunsPolicy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Rejection is the pool's overload behavior. Choosing it deliberately separates people who design for failure from people who accept defaults.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Four built-ins. AbortPolicy (default) throws RejectedExecutionException, which is the honest one: the caller learns it is overloaded. CallerRunsPolicy runs the task on the submitting thread, which slows the producer and acts as crude backpressure. DiscardPolicy silently drops the new task and DiscardOldestPolicy drops the queue head and retries; both lose work silently, so I use them only for best-effort data like metrics samples. Rejection also happens after shutdown(). I choose based on whether the caller can slow down, fail, or lose the task."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rejection triggers in two cases per the ThreadPoolExecutor docs: the executor is shut down, or both the maximum pool size and the bounded queue are saturated.

Policy Behaviour Good for Danger
AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException request paths that can return 503/retry Uncaught -> propagates up the stack; may kill a scheduler thread
CallerRunsPolicy caller runs task (no-op/discard if executor is shut down) internal pipelines where slowing the producer is desired Runs on the caller: may be a Netty event loop, a Kafka poll thread, or a request thread holding a lock
DiscardPolicy silently drops new task telemetry, cache warmers Silent data loss; Future never completes, get() hangs forever
DiscardOldestPolicy drops queue head, resubmits "latest value wins" streams Same silent loss; with a PriorityBlockingQueue it drops the highest priority item

Custom handler: log + metric + throw, or spill to a durable queue. Whatever you pick, count rejections.

CallerRunsPolicy specifics:

  • It provides feedback only if submission is on a thread whose slowdown helps (e.g., the thing feeding the pool). If many threads submit, load is still bounded by their number.
  • If the caller is part of the same pool (task submits subtasks), the worker runs the subtask inline: this avoids a deadlock but grows the stack.
  • The task runs with the caller's thread-locals and security context, a subtle behavior change.
  • Once the pool is shut down, CallerRunsPolicy discards the task without running it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
RejectedExecutionHandler h = (r, ex) -> {
    metrics.counter("pool.rejected", "pool", "pricing").increment();
    throw new RejectedExecutionException("pricing pool saturated: queue="
        + ex.getQueue().size() + " active=" + ex.getActiveCount());
};

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving AbortPolicy and not catching the exception at the submit site.
  • DiscardPolicy with submit() then future.get() (no timeout) -> thread hangs forever.
  • CallerRunsPolicy on a Netty/WebFlux event-loop thread: blocks the loop and makes everything slower.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. HTTP controller submits to a pool; which policy? → Abort, translate to 503 + Retry-After. Fast failure beats a queue that adds latency to every request.
  2. Why can CallerRunsPolicy cause a cascade? → The request thread now does slow work, so the servlet pool drains faster, upstream queues fill, health checks time out.
  3. How do you avoid losing work yet still bound memory? → Spill to a durable queue (Kafka, DB outbox) in a custom handler, or pause the upstream source.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists the four. Senior: ties each to caller context (event loop vs poller vs request), notes silent-hang risk with discard, and insists on metrics/alerts for rejection counts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team switched to CallerRunsPolicy to "stop losing tasks"; under a partner outage their HTTP threads ran the slow calls inline and the whole service went unavailable instead of one feature.

questions.promptHtml: How do you size a thread pool for CPU-bound versus IO-bound work? Give the formula and its limits.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "How many threads?" is the most common practical question. A senior reasons from CPU count and wait/compute ratio, and then validates by measurement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "CPU-bound work: about N cores, maybe N+1, because extra threads just add context switching. IO-bound: more threads, using the Goetz formula threads = cores x target utilization x (1 + wait/compute). With 8 cores, 80% target, and 90 ms waiting per 10 ms of CPU, that is 8 x 0.8 x 10 = 64. It's an estimate: wait/compute varies, downstream capacity caps useful concurrency, and I validate with a load test and watch queue wait."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• CPU-bound: a core can run one thread at a time. More threads than cores adds context switches, cache misses and no throughput. Size to availableProcessors() (container-aware since 8u191/10) or +1.
  • IO-bound: while a thread waits, the core is free. Threads needed so cores stay busy: N_threads = N_cpu x U_cpu x (1 + W/C) (from Java Concurrency in Practice; sources vary on whether U is included, I use it because multiple pools share the machine).
  • Worked example: 4 cores, U = 1, a task is 5 ms CPU + 45 ms DB wait: W/C = 9 -> 4 x 10 = 40 threads. Throughput ceiling: 40 threads / 50 ms = 800 tasks/s, and CPU is 800 x 5 ms = 4 core-seconds per second = 100% of 4 cores. Consistent.
  • Mixed workload: do not mix CPU-bound and IO-bound tasks in one pool; the formula needs one W/C ratio and slow IO tasks starve CPU tasks. Use separate pools (see the bulkhead question).
  • Limits: (1) W/C is not constant: it moves when a dependency slows. (2) Downstream capacity: 64 threads hitting a DB pool of 20 connections just queue on the connection pool. The pool should not exceed the scarcest downstream resource. (3) Memory: each platform thread reserves stack (default 1 MB on 64-bit Linux, -Xss/-XX:ThreadStackSize) mostly virtual until touched. (4) Container CPU limits: 2 vCPU limit with 8 visible host cores can cause CFS throttling if the JVM thinks it has more. (5) Little's law cross-check: concurrency L = throughput x latency.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
double util = 0.8, waitMs = 90, computeMs = 10;
int ioThreads = (int) Math.ceil(cores * util * (1 + waitMs / computeMs)); // 8 cores -> 64
int cpuThreads = cores; // CPU-bound pool

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using "2 x cores" as a universal rule.
  • Sizing a pool larger than the DB/HTTP connection pool it feeds.
  • Measuring W/C once in dev, where dependencies are fast.
  • Forgetting the container: availableProcessors() reflects cgroup limits, but if you set -XX:ActiveProcessorCount or run with fractional CPU quota, recompute.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do virtual threads change this? → For blocking IO you stop sizing pools by W/C and bound concurrency with a semaphore against the downstream limit instead. CPU-bound work still wants ~cores.
  2. How do you validate? → Load test, watch CPU, p99 queue wait (time in queue), and downstream saturation. Increase threads until CPU nears target or downstream latency rises.
  3. 16 cores, task = 1 ms CPU + 99 ms wait, target 70%. → 16 x 0.7 x 100 = 1120 threads in theory; I'd cap by the downstream's limit and consider async/virtual threads rather than 1000+ platform threads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "cores for CPU, more for IO". Senior: formula with a worked number, names the downstream cap, separates pools by workload, and validates under load.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 200-thread pool in front of a 30-connection DB pool added no throughput and tripled p99 because 170 threads sat waiting on Hikari.

questions.contextHtml: You own a REST gateway endpoint POST /quote that, per request, fans out to 3 internal services in parallel: pricing (p50 40 ms, p99 120 ms), inventory (p50 30 ms, p99 90 ms), and tax (p50 10 ms, p99 30 ms). Peak target: 600 requests/s. Each downstream call burns about 1 ms of CPU for serialization. Pod: 4 vCPU, Tomcat with 200 request threads. A colleague proposes one shared newCachedThreadPool() for the fan-out. Another suggests Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) "because we have 4 cores". Production p99 target: 250 ms.
questions.promptHtml: How would you size and structure the fan-out executor(s)? Show the numbers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a number by rule of thumb ("2x cores = 8") or accepts cached because "it scales". Neither considers latency or the downstream.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are downstream calls blocking clients or async? What are the downstream rate limits and connection-pool sizes? Must all three succeed (fail whole request) or can we degrade? Is the fan-out CPU light (it is: ~3 ms per request)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I would at least reject the cached pool, since downstream slowness turns into thread explosion.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (candidate designs): (a) 8 fixed threads, (b) cached, (c) sized by Little's law with bounded queue, (d) per-downstream pools (bulkheads).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute, then load test with k6 at 600, 1200 RPS and with pricing injected at 500 ms.
  5. Root cause / analysis: Calls per second = 600 x 3 = 1800. Concurrency by Little's law, L = rate x latency: pricing 600 x 0.040 = 24 in flight on average (p99: 600 x 0.120 = 72); inventory 600 x 0.030 = 18 (p99 54); tax 600 x 0.010 = 6 (p99 18). Total average 48, p99-ish 144. With 8 threads we can serve 8 / 0.027 (mean per-call ≈ 27 ms) ≈ 300 calls/s, far below 1800 -> queueing explosion. Cached has no upper bound; if pricing goes to 2 s, in-flight pricing = 600 x 2 = 1200 threads (x1 MB reserved stack = 1.2 GB virtual, risk of unable to create native thread on a limited container).
  6. Fix: Per-downstream bulkhead pools sized to peak with headroom: pricing 80, inventory 60, tax 24 (Little at p99 plus ~10% margin), each with a small bounded queue (say 20) and AbortPolicy, mapped to a fast fallback or 503. Add per-call timeouts (pricing 200 ms) and a circuit breaker so a slow pricing cannot use all 80 slots for long. Total ~164 threads at 4 vCPU is fine because they are almost entirely waiting (W/C ≈ 40:1). Check connection pools match: HTTP client max connections per route >= pool size. Alternatively use async clients/virtual threads and bound with semaphores.
ThreadPoolExecutor pricing = new ThreadPoolExecutor(80, 80, 0, SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(20), named("pricing"), new AbortPolicy());
pricing.prestartAllCoreThreads();
  1. Prevention: Metrics per pool: active, queue depth, rejected, task time. Alert when active/max > 80% for 5 min. Chaos test: inject latency into each downstream in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Separate pools cost more idle threads but prevent one slow service from consuming all slots (bulkhead). I would not use one shared pool (head-of-line blocking across services) or the common pool (shared with parallel streams, size ~3 on 4 cores).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Traffic doubles to 1200 RPS? → Pricing p99 in flight = 144; pool 80 rejects. Scale pods horizontally (each carries 600), or raise pool and check pricing's capacity, not just ours.
  • Pricing outage, all calls time out at 200 ms? → In flight 600 x 0.2 = 120 > 80, so rejections begin; circuit breaker opens, we return the cached/default price.
  • Could we cut threads with async I/O? → Yes: with non-blocking clients or virtual threads you drop the per-call thread, and bound with a semaphore sized from the same Little's law result.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a gateway used one shared pool for all downstreams. When a single reporting backend slowed to 3 s, it consumed every thread within a minute, and healthy endpoints timed out too. Splitting pools was a one-day change; the incident review called it the cheapest reliability win of the year.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Rule-of-thumb sizing, accepts cached pool.
  • Hire: Applies Little's law, sets bounded queues, mentions timeouts.
  • Strong hire: Per-downstream bulkheads with numbers at p99, connection-pool alignment, failure-mode load test, and alternatives (async/virtual threads).

questions.promptHtml: Bounded versus unbounded work queues: how do you choose the queue type and size, and how do SynchronousQueue, ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue and PriorityBlockingQueue change pool behavior?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Queue choice defines latency under load, memory risk and fairness. Seniors reason in terms of backpressure and time-in-queue.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The queue is where overload shows up, so I bound it and size it by the latency I can tolerate: queue depth = tolerated wait x service rate. An unbounded queue hides overload as latency and eventually as an OOM. SynchronousQueue is direct hand-off with zero buffering: tasks either get a thread now or the pool grows (needs a large max) or rejects. ArrayBlockingQueue is a fixed ring buffer with one lock; LinkedBlockingQueue can be bounded and uses two locks (put/take) so higher throughput under contention; PriorityBlockingQueue is unbounded, so combine with care. And the true fix for overload is backpressure upstream, not a bigger queue."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Tolerated wait budget: Pool of 20, mean service time 50 ms -> 400 tasks/s. If you can tolerate 500 ms extra latency, the queue depth is 400 x 0.5 = 200. A queue of 100,000 means a 250 s delay before a task even runs, longer than any client timeout, so most of that work is wasted (clients already gave up).
  • Throughput characteristics: LinkedBlockingQueue uses separate putLock/takeLock, so producers and consumers do not contend. ArrayBlockingQueue uses a single ReentrantLock (fair optional) but allocates no nodes, lower GC pressure. For very high rates consider LinkedTransferQueue or a Disruptor (see the collections chunk).
  • SynchronousQueue: capacity 0; offer succeeds only if a consumer is waiting. In newCachedThreadPool this means "reuse an idle thread or create a new one".
  • PriorityBlockingQueue: honors priorities but is unbounded, and Runnables submitted via submit() are wrapped in FutureTask, which is not Comparable; you must use execute() or override newTaskFor. Low-priority tasks can starve.
  • Order of operations again: with a bounded queue and max > core, threads above core appear only after the queue is full; so a large queue delays scale-up. Small queue + larger max = elastic, large queue + core = max = predictable.
  • Backpressure vs buffering: a queue is a shock absorber for bursts (seconds), not for sustained overload. If arrival > service for longer than the queue can absorb, you must shed (reject, drop old, reduce intake).
  • LIFO vs FIFO under overload: in overload, FIFO serves the oldest (likely already timed-out) requests first. Some systems prefer LIFO/adaptive LIFO or drop requests whose deadline has passed at dequeue.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Drop tasks whose deadline already passed
record Job(Runnable body, long deadlineNanos) implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        if (System.nanoTime() > deadlineNanos) { metrics.expired.increment(); return; }
        body.run();
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• new PriorityBlockingQueue with submit(), giving ClassCastException.
  • Choosing queue size = 1000 "because it feels safe".
  • Treating rejected tasks as an error rather than a signal to scale or shed.
  • Forgetting ArrayBlockingQueue fairness flag costs throughput.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would a bigger queue make p99 worse? → Tasks wait longer; throughput is unchanged. You trade failures for latency, and clients retry, adding load.
  2. How do you apply deadline-aware shedding? → Stamp enqueue time, check at dequeue, skip expired work and count it.
  3. How would you monitor "queueing delay" rather than depth? → Wrap tasks to record enqueueNanos and report start - enqueue as a timer (Micrometer); depth alone doesn't convert to time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use bounded queue to avoid OOM". Senior: derives size from latency budget and service rate, explains lock structure and failure semantics of each queue, adds deadline-aware dropping and upstream backpressure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A job runner with a 50k-deep queue worked down items that clients had cancelled 4 minutes earlier, burning DB capacity on dead requests during the recovery.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between execute() and submit(), and what happens to an exception thrown inside a task in each case?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Swallowed exceptions are a leading cause of "the job silently didn't run" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "execute(Runnable) runs the task and any exception propagates to the worker thread: the thread dies, the uncaught exception handler prints it, and the pool starts a replacement. submit() wraps the task in a FutureTask; exceptions are caught and stored, and only surface when you call get() (wrapped in ExecutionException). If you never call get(), the exception disappears without a log line. So with submit, I always keep the Future and handle it, or wrap tasks in try/catch with logging."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• execute is the only method on Executor. submit is on ExecutorService and returns a Future<?> for Runnable or Future<T> for Callable.
  • With submit, FutureTask.run() has try { result = c.call(); } catch (Throwable ex) { setException(ex); }. Nothing is logged and the worker survives.
  • With execute, the throwable escapes runWorker, completedAbruptly = true, the worker is removed and a new thread created, with the default name counter incremented (pool-1-thread-9 etc). The default handler prints Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-3". Thread churn from repeated failures costs a thread creation each time.
  • invokeAll waits for all and returns Futures; invokeAny returns the first successful result and cancels the rest.
  • CompletableFuture.runAsync behaves like submit: exceptions live in the stage until observed (see the CompletableFuture chunk).
  • afterExecute(Runnable, Throwable) in a ThreadPoolExecutor subclass is a hook to log; for submit, the Throwable passed is null and the exception is inside the FutureTask, so you have to unwrap it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("lost"); }); // silent
Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("seen"); });
try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log.error("task failed", e.getCause()); }

pool.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("printed by handler"); });

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fire-and-forget submit for work that can fail.
  • Catching ExecutionException but logging only e.getMessage() (the real stack is the cause).
  • Calling get() without a timeout in a request thread.
  • Expecting scheduleAtFixedRate failures to be visible; they are in the Future (see the scheduling questions).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get uncaught exceptions logged for both paths? → Wrap tasks in a try/catch(Throwable) with logging, or override afterExecute and unwrap FutureTask when t == null.
  2. What does Future.get() throw on cancel and interrupt? → CancellationException; InterruptedException (restore flag); ExecutionException for task failure; TimeoutException with timed get.
  3. Does Future.cancel(true) stop a running task? → It interrupts the worker thread; the task must cooperate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "submit returns a future". Senior: describes where the exception goes, worker replacement, the silent drop, and standardises error logging at the executor boundary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A nightly sync used submit without keeping the Future; a NullPointerException in every task was invisible for three weeks until reconciliation found the gap.

questions.contextHtml: A checkout service (4 vCPU pod, Tomcat maxThreads=200, 12 pods) sends a confirmation email asynchronously via an emailPool: new ThreadPoolExecutor(10,10,0,SECONDS,new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100), new CallerRunsPolicy()). SMTP provider normally replies in 80 ms. At 19:40 the provider starts taking 8 s per call. Checkout traffic is 150 req/s across the fleet (12.5 req/s per pod). By 19:43: checkout p99 goes from 300 ms to 25 s, liveness probes fail, and pods restart in a loop. CPU is 10%, heap is fine. A thread dump from one pod shows 198 of 200 http-nio-8080-exec-* threads in SmtpTransport.sendMessage -> SocketInputStream.socketRead0, and the 10 email-* threads in the same call.
questions.promptHtml: What is the mechanism of the outage, and how do you fix it without losing emails?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "SMTP is slow, so increase the pool or timeouts." That misses that the rejection policy moved slow work into the request path, turning an optional feature into a checkout outage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are emails required for correctness or just notification? Is there a request-level SLA? Does the SMTP client have a read timeout? Do we have an outbox or retry store?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag off sync-ish email sending, or swap to a no-op/queue-to-disk path; scale down the email call concurrency; if the flag does not exist, redeploy with AbortPolicy handled by logging. Pause traffic restarts by relaxing the liveness probe (it should not depend on the downstream anyway).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) CallerRunsPolicy executing SMTP on request threads. (b) No SMTP read timeout. (c) Tomcat thread exhaustion due to something else (DB). (d) GC. The dump shows (a): request threads are inside sendMessage.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack x3 spaced 10 s apart: same frames, not progressing. Micrometer executor_queued_tasks/executor_pool_size for emailPool saturated at 100/10. Arrival math: 12.5 emails/s per pod; service rate 10 threads / 8 s = 1.25/s. Overflow 11.25/s runs on request threads. Within seconds, the 200 request threads are consumed.
  5. Root cause: Capacity of the email stage fell from 125/s to 1.25/s. The queue (100) filled in ~9 s. After that most submits ran inline in a Tomcat thread for 8 s. By Little's law, 11.25 inline emails/s x 8 s = 90 request threads busy in SMTP on average, on top of the normal request work and retries/timeouts from clients, so the 200-thread pool saturates within a minute or two as latency (and client retries) grow. Then the accept queue fills, latency explodes, liveness fails, restart loop. The optional side effect had been coupled to the critical path.
  6. Fix: Short term: AbortPolicy plus catch at the call site (drop to an outbox table or log and move on), SMTP read/connect timeout of 2 s, circuit breaker. Long term: transactional outbox (write email row in the same DB transaction as the order), separate worker drains it with retries and backoff. The email pool is a bulkhead, not a part of the request.
try { emailPool.execute(task); }
catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { outbox.save(email); metrics.counter("email.spilled").increment(); }
  1. Prevention: Alert on queue depth and rejection; synthetic test with 10 s latency injected into SMTP; code review rule: no CallerRunsPolicy on pools invoked from request/event-loop threads; liveness probe checks only process health.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Outbox adds a table and a drain job but gives durability. I would not raise the queue to 100k (memory + stale emails) or rely on DiscardPolicy (lost receipts, legal exposure).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Emails must go out within 1 minute for compliance? → The outbox drain runs on its own schedule with alerting on oldest unsent age.
  • What if you only have CallerRunsPolicy available in a shared library? → Wrap with a decorator executor that catches the saturation first, or submit from a dedicated "dispatcher" thread rather than request threads.
  • Why did liveness make it worse? → Killing pods dropped in-flight requests and concentrated load on remaining pods; liveness should not check dependencies.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a payments team: the notification pool was added as "fire and forget" years earlier. The first provider outage turned it into a hard dependency of checkout. Moving to an outbox cut the checkout path's external dependency count by one and shortened their incident runbook by half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames SMTP only; proposes bigger pool/queue.
  • Hire: Identifies CallerRunsPolicy moving work into request threads; adds timeout and abort.
  • Strong hire: Does the capacity math, explains liveness-probe amplification, designs outbox/bulkhead, and adds prevention (tests, alerts, rule).

questions.promptHtml: How does ForkJoinPool differ from a ThreadPoolExecutor, and how does work stealing work? When is it the right tool?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: FJP underlies parallel streams, CompletableFuture async defaults and RecursiveTask. Interviewers want to see you understand why it suits divide-and-conquer and not blocking calls.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "ForkJoinPool gives each worker its own double-ended deque instead of one shared queue. A worker pushes and pops its own forked subtasks from one end (LIFO, cache-friendly, depth-first), while idle workers steal from the opposite end of other workers' deques (FIFO, taking the biggest, oldest chunks). Fewer contended queue operations means good throughput for many small, CPU-bound, recursively split tasks. A joining worker doesn't sit idle: it runs other tasks while waiting. It is a bad fit for blocking IO because the pool is sized to cores."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Worker A deque:  [t1 t2 t3 t4]  <- owner pushes/pops here (LIFO)
                  ^ thieves take from the other end (FIFO)
Worker B (idle) steals t1 (oldest = usually largest unsplit chunk)
  • Fork: push subtask on own deque. Join: if the subtask is still unstolen, run it directly; otherwise help by running other tasks (or briefly compensating) until it completes. This "helping" is why a small pool can run deep recursion without deadlock.
  • Parallelism: the pool targets N active threads; ForkJoinPool.managedBlock with a ManagedBlocker lets a blocking task tell the pool to add a compensating thread. Phaser, CompletableFuture.get, and some JDK blocking paths use it. Plain Thread.sleep or JDBC calls do not, so those starve the pool.
  • Tasks: RecursiveTask<V> (result), RecursiveAction (void), CountedCompleter. Threshold choice matters: split until a chunk costs roughly 100 µs-1 ms of work or less benefit than overhead.
  • Async mode (asyncMode=true) uses FIFO for event-style tasks that are never joined.
  • Executors.newWorkStealingPool() builds an FJP with parallelism = availableProcessors(); its threads are daemon.
  • Compare: a TPE has one queue and any worker takes the head. Great for independent tasks of mixed duration with predictable semantics; FJP is optimised for fine-grained subtasks that spawn subtasks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    final long[] a; final int lo, hi;
    SumTask(long[] a, int lo, int hi) { this.a = a; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi; }
    protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= 10_000) { long s = 0; for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) s += a[i]; return s; }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        var left = new SumTask(a, lo, mid);
        left.fork();                              // async
        long right = new SumTask(a, mid, hi).compute(); // reuse this thread
        return right + left.join();
    }
}
long total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(arr, 0, arr.length));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forking both halves and joining both: wastes the current thread; compute one half directly.
  • Blocking IO inside compute().
  • Threshold too small (overhead) or too large (no parallelism).
  • Assuming FJP preserves submission order.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why steal from the opposite end? → Reduces contention with the owner, and old tasks are larger so each steal moves more work.
  2. What is the common pool's default parallelism? → availableProcessors() - 1 (calling thread helps), overridable with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism; the minimum is 1 per the JDK issue discussions I found; verify on your JDK.
  3. How does a task block safely in FJP? → ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(blocker), which lets the pool spawn compensating threads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "work stealing, used by parallel streams". Senior: explains deque ends, join helping, managed blocking, and why it is wrong for blocking IO.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A recursive document-processing task using RecursiveTask plus blocking S3 reads on the common pool froze unrelated parallelStream() calls in the same JVM.

questions.promptHtml: What are the pitfalls of parallelStream() in a backend service? Which pool does it use and how can one stream hurt the rest of the application?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: parallelStream() is easy to write and hard to operate. It is a frequent source of production incidents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Parallel streams run on the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), sized availableProcessors() - 1 by default, and the caller thread participates too. That pool is JVM-wide: every parallel stream, and by default every CompletableFuture.*Async without an executor, shares it. Blocking IO or a long-running job in one stream starves everything else. Other pitfalls: tiny workloads are slower than sequential due to split/merge overhead, non-thread-safe accumulators, ordered operations that kill parallelism, and thread-locals not propagating to pool threads. In a request path I usually avoid parallel streams and use an explicit executor."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The stream is split by the source's Spliterator. ArrayList and arrays split well (indexed). LinkedList, Stream.iterate, BufferedReader.lines() split poorly.
  • Cost model rule of thumb (N x Q): parallel pays off when elements x per-element cost is large (roughly N x Q > 10,000 "operations"), the source splits cheaply, and the operations are stateless, non-interfering and CPU-bound.
  • Operations like limit, skip, findFirst, forEachOrdered, sorted and ordered collect can force coordination, buffering, or limit the speedup.
  • Reduction must be associative; reduce(identity, accumulator, combiner) with an identity that is not an identity yields wrong results in parallel. Use Collectors, not forEach into a shared ArrayList.
  • Common pool is also what a CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(...) uses if you pass no executor (when parallelism > 1; otherwise it spawns a thread per task).
  • Isolation workaround: submit the terminal operation from inside a custom ForkJoinPool (pool.submit(() -> list.parallelStream()...).get()). It works in practice because tasks fork into the current worker's pool, but that behavior is an implementation detail and is not specified by the stream contract. Prefer plain executors with futures for IO.
  • Thread-locals (MDC, security context, transaction) are not available in common-pool threads, and worse, the calling thread does have them, so behavior differs between the elements it processes and the elements others do.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: shared mutable state + blocking IO on the common pool
List<Result> out = new ArrayList<>();
ids.parallelStream().forEach(id -> out.add(httpClient.fetch(id))); // race + starvation

// Better: bounded executor for IO, collect safely
var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
List<CompletableFuture<Result>> fs = ids.stream()
    .map(id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.fetch(id), pool)).toList();
List<Result> out2 = fs.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "parallel is always faster": a 100-element list of cheap ops is slower in parallel.
  • Using parallelStream inside a web request on a 2-vCPU container: common pool parallelism is 1 plus the caller.
  • Nested parallel streams.
  • Relying on thread names or order.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you change common pool size? → -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N at startup; JVM-wide, so affects every library.
  2. Why is a pool of cores - 1 the default? → The submitting thread also executes tasks, so total active equals cores.
  3. How do you prove a parallel stream is worth it? → JMH benchmark with realistic data size and container CPU; and test under concurrent load, since in a server several streams contend for the same workers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "uses ForkJoinPool, can be faster". Senior: names the shared pool, the CPU-only rule, ordering/associativity traps, thread-local loss, container CPU effect, and prefers explicit executors with bounded concurrency for IO.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A single parallelStream() doing HTTP calls inside a REST handler throttled to 3 workers on a 4-core pod and starved an unrelated scheduled job that used supplyAsync on the common pool.

questions.contextHtml:
A recommendation service (pods: 4 vCPU, 4 GB, Java 17) serves GET /home with p99 of 180 ms. After release 2.14 on Tuesday, p99 spikes to 9 s every 10 minutes for about 90 seconds, and returns to normal. CPU stays at 25%; no GC anomalies (young pauses < 30 ms). The release added a "fraud-score refresh" job, which every 10 minutes runs:

List<Account> accts = repo.findFlagged(); // ~3,000 rows
accts.parallelStream().forEach(a -> fraudClient.score(a)); // HTTP call, ~120 ms each

Request handlers also call CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> profileService.load(id)) with no executor, and they use .parallelStream() for layout assembly. Thread dump during a spike shows 3 ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-* threads in SocketInputStream.socketRead0 (inside fraudClient.score) and a pile of http-nio-exec threads in CompletableFuture.get.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. What does the arithmetic tell you about the 90 seconds?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the fraud client timeout" or "add more CPU". Does not link the job to the shared pool; ignores that CPU is idle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the common pool parallelism on these pods? Does the 10-minute interval align with the job schedule? Do any other call paths use async/parallel stream defaults? Are the spikes on all pods simultaneously?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable or throttle the refresh job (feature flag), or run it on a separate pod/CronJob. Restart is pointless since it will recur.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Refresh job occupies the common pool with blocking IO. (b) fraudClient is slow. (c) DB slow. (d) Request thread exhaustion for another reason. (a) fits idle CPU + 10-minute periodicity + dump.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.print during a spike: all commonPool-worker-1..3 in fraudClient.score; ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism() via a JMX/JFR check or log at startup shows 3 (4 cores - 1). JFR "Java Monitor/Socket Read" events attribute time to those threads. Arithmetic: 3,000 calls x 0.12 s = 360 thread-seconds; with 4 effective workers (3 + caller) ≈ 90 s. That is exactly the observed spike length.
  5. Root cause: The job occupies all common pool workers for ~90 s; supplyAsync and parallelStream in request handlers queue behind it. Request threads block on get() (hence the 9 s timeouts), with no CPU use.
  6. Fix: Short term: move the refresh to its own bounded executor (e.g. 8 threads, which finishes 3,000 calls in 3000 x 0.12 / 8 = 45 s) and respect fraudClient's rate limit. Long term: pass explicit executors to every supplyAsync call, forbid common-pool defaults via lint, make the job a batch outside the serving path.
var fraudPool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),
    named("fraud-refresh"), new CallerRunsPolicy()); // runs on the scheduler thread, fine here
for (Account a : accts) fraudPool.execute(() -> fraudClient.score(a));
  1. Prevention: -XX:+FlightRecorder, or log common pool stats (getActiveThreadCount, getQueuedSubmissionCount) to metrics; ArchUnit/Error Prone rule: no supplyAsync without executor; load test with a slow downstream.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Raising ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism to 32 would "fix" it but moves a global JVM setting and still lets any future job starve requests. Wrapping the stream in a custom FJP works but relies on unspecified behavior.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why do p99 spikes not show in average latency? → Only requests during the 90 s windows (15% of time) are affected; average hides it, the p99 does not.
  • What if fraudClient rate-limits at 20 calls/s? → The pool of 8 would exceed the limit (66/s). Use a rate limiter or reduce to 2 threads; job takes 150 s but nobody waits.
  • Could you use virtual threads here? → Yes for the job's IO, bounded by a semaphore matching the rate limit; but the common pool use in handlers would still need its own fix.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "harmless" analytics parallelStream in a cache-warmer saturated the common pool on every node every hour. The team spent a week blaming the DB because CPU was idle; the thread dump took five minutes once someone looked.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: No link to the shared pool; suggests more CPU.
  • Hire: Finds common pool starvation from blocking IO and moves the job to a dedicated executor.
  • Strong hire: Does the 360 thread-second arithmetic, verifies via dump/JFR, adds lint and metrics, and respects downstream rate limits.

questions.promptHtml: Explain schedule, scheduleAtFixedRate and scheduleWithFixedDelay. What happens if a run takes longer than the period or throws?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The silent-stop-on-exception behavior and overlapping semantics are frequent bugs in housekeeping jobs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "schedule runs once after a delay. scheduleAtFixedRate(initial, period) tries to start runs at start times initial + n x period; if a run overruns, later runs start late but never overlap each other. scheduleWithFixedDelay(initial, delay) waits delay after each run finishes, so there is never a catch-up. If a periodic task throws, the exception is captured in the Future and all subsequent runs are suppressed, silently unless you check the Future or catch inside the task."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor (STPE) uses a DelayedWorkQueue, a heap ordered by trigger time. It is unbounded; maximumPoolSize is effectively ignored since the queue never rejects.
  • Fixed rate: next start = previous scheduled start + period (anchored to schedule). A 5 s task with a 1 s period runs back-to-back, never concurrently, and stays behind. After a long GC pause or suspended VM, missed executions are not "replayed in parallel" but executed one after another as soon as possible.
  • Fixed delay: next start = last end + delay. Use it when runs must not pile up or when you want a rest period (e.g., polling).
  • Timing is based on System.nanoTime(), so it's immune to wall-clock changes but not DST/cron-like. For "every day at 02:00" you need cron semantics (Quartz/Spring @Scheduled(cron)), not STPE.
  • Single-thread scheduler: one slow task delays all other tasks sharing it. Spring's default @Scheduled scheduler is a single thread unless configured (spring.task.scheduling.pool.size, default 1).
  • Cancelled tasks stay in the queue until their delay expires unless setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true) (memory growth when scheduling many timeouts and cancelling them).
  • On shutdown, getContinueExistingPeriodicTasksAfterShutdownPolicy default false: periodic tasks cancel on shutdown(); delayed one-shots run by default.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var sched = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);
sched.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> { // exception kills the schedule
    try { syncOnce(); } catch (Throwable t) { log.error("sync failed", t); }
}, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting an exception escape a periodic task.
  • Using fixed rate for a job whose runtime can exceed the period (catch-up storm).
  • One shared single-thread scheduler for unrelated jobs.
  • Using STPE for wall-clock schedules.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. FixedRate period 1 s, task takes 3 s: what runs? → One run at a time, back-to-back (each starting as soon as the last ends), so effectively every 3 s but "behind".
  2. How do you make a cron job exactly once across 5 pods? → Distributed lock (ShedLock, DB advisory lock, K8s CronJob); STPE is per-JVM.
  3. Why can cancelled timeouts leak memory? → They stay in the heap-ordered queue until due; use setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: the three method names. Senior: overrun semantics, silent suppression, queue behavior, single-thread coupling, and why multi-instance needs distributed coordination.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache-refresh job died on the first transient exception on Monday and nobody noticed until stale prices were served on Thursday.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service refreshes an in-memory exchange-rate map every minute. In staging it works. In production, rates freeze about once every few weeks: ratesAge metric climbs and no errors appear in logs after the last successful refresh. Thread dump shows the scheduler thread rates-1 idle in DelayedWorkQueue.take. The code:

class RateRefresher {
    private final ScheduledExecutorService ses =
        Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "rates"));
    private volatile Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = Map.of();

    void start() {
        ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::refresh, 0, 1, TimeUnit.MINUTES);
    }
    void refresh() {
        var fresh = client.fetchAll();      // may throw on 5xx / timeout
        rates = Map.copyOf(fresh);
    }
}

The provider returned HTTP 503 for a few seconds last night. Heap, CPU and GC are normal.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why there are no logs, and fix it properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably a network issue; add retries to the client." Misses that any exception cancels the periodic schedule itself.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When exactly did the last refresh happen vs the 503? Is the scheduler the only thing producing ratesAge? Is there any monitoring on the returned Future?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart the instance (or trigger a manual refresh via an admin endpoint) so rates resume; flag rates as stale in responses if age > threshold.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Exception in refresh suppressed the schedule. (b) Thread died or hung. (c) Deadlock. (d) Clock issue. The idle scheduler thread in DelayedWorkQueue.take with no pending task points to (a): queue empty means no future runs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dump shows thread alive but queue empty, so nothing is scheduled. Reproduce with a stub client that throws once: second run never happens. Check ScheduledFuture.isDone() on the saved future: true.
  5. Root cause: Per ScheduledExecutorService contract, if any execution of a periodic task throws, subsequent executions are suppressed. The exception is stored in the ScheduledFutureTask, never logged because nobody calls get(). The thread stays alive and idle.
  6. Fix: Catch Throwable inside the task (log + metric), keep the last good value, and add staleness alerting. Consider fixed delay so a slow provider does not trigger back-to-back catch-up.
void refresh() {
    try {
        rates = Map.copyOf(client.fetchAll());
        lastOk.set(Instant.now());
    } catch (Throwable t) {   // includes Error subclasses we choose to survive
        log.error("rate refresh failed, serving stale rates", t);
        failures.increment();
    }
}
ses.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refresh, 0, 1, TimeUnit.MINUTES);
  1. Prevention: Alert on ratesAge > 5 min, test "refresh throws once, then succeeds", wrap all scheduled tasks via a common SafeRunnable, keep the Future and watch isDone.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Catching Throwable swallows OutOfMemoryError, so I would catch Exception plus log Error and rethrow if it is fatal. I would not restart the scheduler on a timer blindly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should we serve stale rates indefinitely? → No; define max staleness; beyond it fail closed or fall back to a secondary source.
  • Why does ratesAge matter more than error logs? → Because the failure mode here is the absence of logs. Alert on missing success, not only on errors.
  • volatile on the map: needed? → Yes for safe publication of the reference; Map.copyOf gives an immutable snapshot so readers need no lock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a limits-cache job died after a single null response, and customers hit stale limits for four days. The fix was one try/catch, the lesson was to alert on "time since last success".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests network retries, misses the suppression semantics.
  • Hire: Identifies the exception cancelling subsequent runs; adds try/catch.
  • Strong hire: Adds staleness metric, fixed delay choice, Error handling nuance, and a regression test.

questions.promptHtml: What are the pitfalls of ThreadLocal with thread pools? Explain both data leakage between requests and memory leaks, and how InheritableThreadLocal behaves with pools.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: ThreadLocals carry user identity, tenant and MDC context. Bugs are security incidents or slow memory leaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A ThreadLocal value lives as long as its thread. Pool threads live for the process, so a value set while handling request A is still there when request B runs on the same thread unless someone calls remove(). That gives cross-request data bleed (wrong tenant, stale user) and memory retention. The map holds weak keys but strong values, so when the ThreadLocal object itself becomes unreachable the entry's key is cleared, but its value stays until the map happens to clean the stale entry. InheritableThreadLocal copies the parent's value only when a thread is created, so pool threads capture a stale snapshot from whichever thread triggered their creation. The rule: set and remove() in try/finally at the task boundary."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Each Thread has a ThreadLocalMap (open-addressing table of Entry extends WeakReference<ThreadLocal<?>> with a strong value). Access is Thread.currentThread().threadLocals.get(this): no locking, fast.
  • Leak mechanism: if the ThreadLocal object is a static field it never becomes unreachable, so every thread keeps its value for the thread's life. If it is non-static and later GC'd, the key goes null but the value is still strongly referenced until expungeStaleEntries during a later set/get/remove on that thread. Idle pool threads may never run that.
  • Classloader leaks: in app servers, a value (or key) whose class comes from the webapp classloader, held in a container thread's map, pins the classloader after undeploy; Tomcat documents this pattern in its memory-leak protection notes and renews pool threads to mitigate (Tomcat 7.0.6+). A custom executor of your own gets no such help.
  • Data bleed: a filter sets TENANT.set(t) and an exception skips the cleanup; the next request sees that tenant.
  • Large values: caching a 10 MB buffer per thread across 200 threads = 2 GB retained.
  • Pool + async hand-off: the context set on the submitting thread is not visible in the worker thread. Context must be captured and re-set (wrapping Runnables, Spring TaskDecorator, Micrometer context-propagation, MDC copying). See the CompletableFuture chunk for the async propagation story.
  • InheritableThreadLocal: childValue copies at thread construction. A pool creates workers lazily, so worker 3 inherits the value of whichever request thread submitted the task that created it, then keeps it forever. Don't use it with pools.
  • Virtual threads support ThreadLocal but millions of them multiply per-thread copies; see the virtual threads chunk for ScopedValue.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT = new ThreadLocal<>();

void handle(Request r) {
    TENANT.set(r.tenant());
    try {
        service.process(r);
    } finally {
        TENANT.remove();   // mandatory in pooled threads
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• set in a filter/interceptor, remove only on the happy path.
  • Per-thread SimpleDateFormat/buffer caches with large sizes in 500-thread pools.
  • Assuming ThreadLocal values follow tasks across executor.submit.
  • Relying on weak keys to prevent leaks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does static final ThreadLocal not leak the ThreadLocal itself? → There's only one object; the leak is the values per thread, bounded by pool size, but still retained.
  2. How do you propagate MDC to async tasks? → Wrap/decorate the Runnable to copy the context map and clear afterwards; frameworks provide TaskDecorator.
  3. Alternatives? → Pass context as a parameter, request-scoped beans, ScopedValue (preview in Java 21; check status per release).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "ThreadLocal can leak, call remove". Senior: explains the weak-key/strong-value map, stale entry expunging, classloader pinning, data bleed as a security issue, and the inheritable pitfall.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A multi-tenant API leaked the previous tenant's ID into logs and DB filters after an exception path skipped remove(); a pen-test found it.

questions.contextHtml:
A WAR-deployed service on Tomcat (Java 17, -Xmx2g, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m) is hot-redeployed twice a day by an internal tool. After about 6 redeploys the node logs java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace; metaspace used climbs ~40 MB per redeploy and never drops. Tomcat's catalina.out also shows on undeploy: The web application [orders] created a ThreadLocal with key of type [com.acme.RequestCtx$1] ... but failed to remove it when the web application was stopped. Threads are going to be renewed over time to try and avoid a probable memory leak. Separately, users occasionally report seeing another user's locale in emails. Heap is stable at ~900 MB.

public final class RequestCtx {
    private static final ThreadLocal<Ctx> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>() {
        @Override protected Ctx initialValue() { return new Ctx(); }
    };
    public static Ctx get() { return CURRENT.get(); }
}
// Filter: no remove() anywhere. Also an app-owned executor:
static final ExecutorService MAIL = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms with one root cause, and how you would prove and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise MaxMetaspaceSize to 1g." That postpones the OOM and ignores the cross-user data bleed, which is a security bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the problem scale with redeploys (classloader) or with uptime? Does the executor get shut down on undeploy? Is the locale bleed on the async mail path or request path? Which Tomcat version (thread renewal exists since 7.0.6)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop hot redeploys; do a full process restart per release; temporarily raise metaspace as a bridge only. For the bleed: disable the async mail path using the context or force explicit locale parameters.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ThreadLocal value/key class from the webapp classloader remains reachable from long-lived threads (container threads or the app's own MAIL pool threads), pinning the classloader and all its classes. (b) JDBC driver registered from webapp. (c) Static caches in shared libs. (d) Logging framework. The Tomcat warning names (a).
  4.
