How I'd verify each: Heap dump after 3 redeploys; in Eclipse MAT, list WebappClassLoaderBase instances (expect 1 live loader; several means a leak) and run "Path to GC roots, exclude weak/soft refs" for an old loader: path ends at Thread -> threadLocals -> ThreadLocalMap$Entry.value -> Ctx -> class -> loader. jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace and jcmd <pid> GC.class_stats (or jmap -clstats) show loaded class growth. jstack shows pool-N-thread-* of MAIL still alive after undeploy.
  5. Root cause: ThreadLocal values are strongly held by thread-owned maps. The MAIL pool and the container's threads outlive the webapp; their maps hold Ctx objects (and the anonymous ThreadLocal subclass), whose classes belong to the webapp loader, so the loader and all its classes cannot be unloaded. Same missing remove() means a pooled thread keeps the last request's Ctx; initialValue never re-runs, so the next request on that thread sees stale locale (data bleed). The MAIL pool is non-daemon and never shut down on undeploy.
  6. Fix: Short term: finally { CURRENT.remove(); } in the filter and around each mail task; shut down MAIL in a ServletContextListener.contextDestroyed (shutdown + awaitTermination, then shutdownNow). Long term: avoid thread-local context where a parameter works; if needed, use a task decorator that sets and clears context; ensure the ThreadLocal type is a JDK class (e.g. ThreadLocal<String>) where possible to avoid pinning a webapp class.
@Override public void destroy() { MAIL.shutdown(); try {
    if (!MAIL.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) MAIL.shutdownNow();
} catch (InterruptedException e) { MAIL.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }
  1. Prevention: Integration test that deploys/undeploys 5 times and asserts classloader count via a heap histogram; Tomcat's JreMemoryLeakPreventionListener and leak-detection logs treated as release blockers; lint for ThreadLocal without remove.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd stop hot redeploys in prod: blue/green with process restart is cheaper than chasing classloader leaks from every library. I would not enable the old unsafe reflective "clear thread locals" hacks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Heap is fine, why does it OOM in Metaspace? → Classes and their metadata live in native metaspace, not heap; a pinned loader retains them even when objects are small.
  • Does Tomcat renewing threads fix MAIL too? → No; only its own pool threads. App-owned executors must be shut down by the app.
  • Would virtual threads help? → They don't fix retention; they give each short-lived virtual thread its own map that dies with it, but a platform-thread pool still leaks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team spent two sprints raising metaspace limits across the fleet before one engineer opened a heap dump and followed a single GC-root path to a ThreadLocal in a logging helper.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises metaspace limits.
  • Hire: Connects ThreadLocal to classloader pinning and data bleed; adds remove() and executor shutdown.
  • Strong hire: Proves it with MAT root paths, notes Tomcat's partial mitigation, designs redeploy test and policy to avoid hot redeploys.

questions.promptHtml: How do you shut down an ExecutorService gracefully? Explain shutdown, shutdownNow, awaitTermination and what changed with close() in Java 19+.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shutdown correctness determines whether deploys lose work, hang or exceed Kubernetes grace periods.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Two-phase: shutdown() stops accepting new tasks and lets queued and running ones finish; awaitTermination(timeout) waits; if it times out, shutdownNow() interrupts workers, drains the queue and returns the tasks that never started; then wait again. Restore the interrupt flag if I am interrupted while waiting. In Java 19+ ExecutorService is AutoCloseable: close() does shutdown plus an untimed wait, and if the caller is interrupted it does shutdownNow, so try-with-resources works for scoped pools."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• shutdown(): orderly; previously submitted tasks run; new submits are rejected. Non-blocking, idempotent.
  • shutdownNow(): attempts to stop actively running tasks (via interrupt), removes and returns queued ones. Tasks that ignore interrupts continue; isTerminating() stays true.
  • awaitTermination blocks until terminated, timeout or interrupt.
  • The reference pattern from the ExecutorService javadoc is the two-phase one (shown below).
  • close() (19+, final in 21): waits indefinitely, so pair it with a deadline if you can't tolerate hanging. Do not use it with a long-lived shared pool.
  • Process level: the JVM's shutdown hooks run on SIGTERM; non-daemon pool threads do not block System.exit, but a main-thread-wait does. In Kubernetes the pod gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s). Your drain budget must be below that, and stop taking traffic first (readiness fail + preStop delay).
  • Spring: ThreadPoolTaskExecutor.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true) and setAwaitTerminationSeconds(n); Spring Boot's server.shutdown=graceful drains HTTP requests (default phase timeout 30 s, verify for your version). Order matters: stop intake, drain executors, then close DB pools and clients.
  • Drop-in rule: shutdownNow() loses queued work unless you persist what it returns.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static void shutdownAndAwait(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace) {
    pool.shutdown();
    try {
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
            List<Runnable> dropped = pool.shutdownNow();
            log.warn("forced shutdown, {} tasks never started", dropped.size());
            pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        pool.shutdownNow();
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only calling shutdown() and exiting main, with nothing waiting for completion.
  • Calling shutdownNow() first, losing queued tasks.
  • Draining executors after closing the DB pool they use.
  • Total drain time exceeding the pod grace period (SIGKILL mid-task).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you avoid losing queued tasks on forced shutdown? → Persist the returned list or, better, make work durable (outbox/queue) and idempotent.
  2. What if tasks ignore interrupts? → Fix them; set per-task deadlines; ultimately rely on idempotency since SIGKILL will come.
  3. In what order do you shut down a service? → Fail readiness, wait for LB deregistration, stop consumers/schedulers, drain executors, flush producers/telemetry, close DB pools.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "call shutdown then awaitTermination". Senior: two-phase with interrupt restore, close() semantics, ordering with the rest of the lifecycle, and the Kubernetes grace-period budget.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Services that "gracefully" waited 60 s on a 30 s grace period were SIGKILLed mid-batch, leaving half-written output on every deploy.

questions.contextHtml:
A payment-reconciliation service (Kubernetes, 10 pods, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30) processes events from a queue via a ThreadPoolExecutor(16,16, ArrayBlockingQueue(2000)). Each task takes 200 ms to 6 s (p99 10 s). Each deploy replaces pods one at a time. Since moving to Java 21 and Spring Boot with default settings, after every deploy reconciliation finds 20-60 events marked processed in the queue but with no ledger entry. Shutdown code today:

@PreDestroy void stop() { pool.shutdownNow(); }

Logs at SIGTERM: Stopping service, then several java.lang.InterruptedException stack traces in LedgerClient.post, then silence. The consumer acks the message when it is handed to the pool.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the losses and propose a shutdown and delivery design that makes deploys lossless.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use shutdown() instead of shutdownNow()." Better, but ignores ack-on-handoff, the grace period budget and in-flight work beyond 30 s.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ledger posting idempotent (idempotency key)? What delivery guarantee does the queue provide? Is ack at-handoff a deliberate choice? How long is p99 of a task vs 30 s? Is the preStop hook configured?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds to 60, add a preStop sleep of ~10 s so the endpoint is removed from LB before SIGTERM processing begins, and replace shutdownNow with a graceful drain. Reconcile and replay the missing events from the queue's audit log.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) shutdownNow interrupts 16 running tasks, the ledger post fails mid-flight; their messages were already acked. (b) Up to 2000 queued tasks are dropped, never started (returned list ignored), also already acked. (c) SIGKILL at 30 s. (d) Duplicate processing. Counting: 16 running + queue; losses of 20-60 suggests running tasks plus a partial queue at the time of kill.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log shutdownNow()'s returned list size and active count; kubectl events for Killing and exit code 137 (SIGKILL) vs 143 (SIGTERM clean); trace one lost event ID in the queue ack log vs ledger; reproduce in staging by SIGTERM under load with k6.
  5. Root cause: Ack-on-handoff means the queue believes the message is done once it enters the in-memory executor queue. Any shutdown path that discards in-memory work (shutdownNow, SIGKILL, crash) destroys acked work. Interrupting a mid-flight network call leaves the ledger outcome unknown.
  6. Fix: (1) Ack after the ledger commit (at-least-once) and make posting idempotent via event ID. (2) On SIGTERM: stop the consumer from polling (pause, no more handoffs), shutdown(), awaitTermination(25 s) (inside the 30 s grace, or 55 s of a 60 s grace), then shutdownNow() and do not ack the unfinished events so the broker redelivers. (3) Cap the executor queue at a size the drain can handle: at 16 threads x ~1 s mean = 16 tasks/s, a 2000 queue would take 125 s to drain; shrink to ~200 (≈12 s) so the drain fits.
consumer.pause();            // stop intake first
pool.shutdown();
if (!pool.awaitTermination(25, SECONDS)) { pool.shutdownNow(); }
// unacked messages are redelivered to the next pod
  1. Prevention: A deploy test that sends SIGTERM during sustained load and asserts zero missing ledger entries; metric for "tasks in flight at shutdown"; alert on exit code 137.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: At-least-once needs idempotency (extra key store). Longer grace periods slow rollouts. I would not extend grace to many minutes as a substitute for durable delivery or keep a 2000-deep in-memory queue of acked work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A task takes 10 s p99 but drain budget is 25 s; some will not finish. → They stay unacked and get redelivered; idempotency absorbs the duplicates.
  • Pod receives requests after SIGTERM? → Endpoint removal races SIGTERM; a preStop sleep and readiness flip cover it.
  • How would an HTTP-driven (not queue-driven) service differ? → Use graceful server shutdown (drain in-flight requests) and make clients retry idempotent calls.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team ran "gracefully" for months because deploys were rare and queues empty at night. Moving to daily daytime deploys exposed the ack-before-work design; the real fix was changing the ack point, not the shutdown code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Swaps to shutdown() only.
  • Hire: Notes ack-on-handoff, adds drain with awaitTermination and grace-period alignment.
  • Strong hire: Idempotent at-least-once design, consumer pause ordering, queue sizing vs drain time, preStop/readiness handling, and a SIGTERM-under-load test.

questions.promptHtml: Why should every thread pool have a custom ThreadFactory, and what should it set? Mention naming, daemon status and uncaught exception handling.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Thread names are the first thing you read in jstack, logs and profilers. This is a cheap hygiene check for production maturity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The default factory names threads pool-N-thread-M, which tells you nothing in a dump. A custom ThreadFactory gives a meaningful prefix like orders-http-%d, sets daemon status deliberately, sets an UncaughtExceptionHandler so failures are logged, and optionally sets priority and a thread group. With names I can match a CPU-hot thread from top -H to its pool in seconds, and filter logs and metrics per pool."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Defaults: Executors.defaultThreadFactory() creates non-daemon, normal-priority threads named pool-<poolNumber>-thread-<n>; poolNumber is a global counter, so numbers change across restarts/ordering.
  • What to set: a stable prefix, an incrementing index, daemon true/false chosen consciously (false for must-finish work), an uncaught handler that logs with context and increments a metric.
  • Where to find helpers: Guava ThreadFactoryBuilder.setNameFormat("orders-%d").setDaemon(false).setUncaughtExceptionHandler(...), Spring CustomizableThreadFactory("orders-"), or a 6-line lambda.
  • Uncaught handlers only see exceptions that escape run(): tasks submitted with execute(); tasks from submit() store exceptions in the Future.
  • Thread names also show up in JFR, async-profiler flame graphs (thread filter), and Thread.getName() MDC/log pattern %t.
  • Dumps can be searched with grep 'orders-'; per-pool stack aggregates become possible.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static ThreadFactory named(String prefix) {
    AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger();
    return r -> {
        Thread t = new Thread(r, prefix + "-" + n.incrementAndGet());
        t.setDaemon(false);
        t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, ex) -> log.error("uncaught in {}", th.getName(), ex));
        return t;
    };
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving pool-1-thread-3 and trying to infer ownership from the stack.
  • Setting a handler and expecting it to catch submit() exceptions.
  • Making all threads daemon by default.
  • Using duplicate prefixes for different pools.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where else can you set a global handler? → Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler for the whole JVM.
  2. How do you map a hot OS thread to a Java thread? → top -H -p PID, convert TID to hex, match nid=0x... in jstack.
  3. Why might per-pool naming matter for metrics? → Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics tags by a name you supply, and names align dumps with dashboards.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "give threads a name". Senior: also daemon policy, uncaught handler limits (execute vs submit), tooling use (nid mapping, flame graph filters), and standardising a factory.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During an incident 11 different anonymous pools were all pool-N-thread-M; it took 40 minutes to learn which one was saturated, five minutes once names were added.

questions.promptHtml: What would you monitor on every thread pool in production, which signals indicate saturation before users notice, and how do you instrument it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Pool problems are silent: CPU is idle while latency explodes. The signal choice shows operational maturity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Per pool I track active threads versus max, pool size, queue depth and remaining capacity, completed tasks, rejections, and most importantly queue wait time and task run time as timers. Saturation shows up as active/max near 1 and a growing queue; depth alone is ambiguous without service rate, so I alert on queue wait p99 and on sustained active ratio. Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics exposes the basics for a ThreadPoolExecutor; I add a custom rejection counter and a wrapper timing enqueue-to-start."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Raw ThreadPoolExecutor getters: getPoolSize(), getActiveCount() (approximate), getLargestPoolSize(), getQueue().size(), remainingCapacity(), getCompletedTaskCount(), getTaskCount().
  • Micrometer ExecutorServiceMetrics.monitor(registry, executor, "orders") binds gauges such as executor.active, executor.queued, executor.pool.size, executor.pool.core, executor.pool.max, executor.queue.remaining, plus executor.completed and executor.seconds / executor.idle timers; the exact set depends on the Micrometer version (verify in your version). Prometheus names appear as executor_active_threads, executor_queued_tasks, etc.
  • Saturation signals:
    • active / max >= 0.8 sustained: the pool is the bottleneck.
    • Queue depth rising while completions flat.
    • Rejections > 0.
    • Queue wait time: wrap each task with submitNanos and record start - submit. By Little's law, queue depth / throughput = wait, but measuring directly is easy and honest.
  • Utilization vs saturation vs errors (USE): utilization = active/max; saturation = queue/wait; errors = rejections and task failures.
  • Use beforeExecute/afterExecute hooks in a subclass for task timing without changing callers.
  • Also watch: thread count (jvm.threads.live), blocked threads, and per-pool thread dump snapshots by name.
  • Pitfall: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() and CompletableFuture async stages are easily missed; Micrometer does register ForkJoinPool metrics (ForkJoinPoolMetrics/ monitor(registry, ForkJoinPool)) in recent versions. Verify availability.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(/* ... */);
new ExecutorServiceMetrics(pool, "orders", List.of()).bindTo(registry);

class TimedTask implements Runnable {
    final Runnable d; final long enq = System.nanoTime();
    TimedTask(Runnable d) { this.d = d; }
    public void run() {
        queueWait.record(System.nanoTime() - enq, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
        d.run();
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Alerting on CPU only. Pools saturate on IO wait with CPU idle.
  • Alerting on queue size with no relation to capacity.
  • Not wrapping Spring-managed executors, so they never appear on a dashboard.
  • Using getActiveCount() as exact; it is a snapshot approximation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Alert thresholds? → Active ratio > 0.8 for 5 min, queue wait p99 above the SLO share, any rejection rate > 0 for pools with abort policy.
  2. How do you tell if a full pool is a downstream problem? → Task time p99 rising across all tasks plus dependency latency metrics up; cross-check with thread dump frames.
  3. How do you observe pools you don't own (library-internal)? → Thread name pattern in dumps, JFR thread statistics, jcmd Thread.print sampling, or ask the library to accept an executor.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "monitor queue size". Senior: separates utilization, saturation and errors; measures queue wait time; wraps tasks; covers hidden pools like the common pool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Dashboards showed healthy CPU during a 20-minute degradation; only after adding queue-wait timers did the team see tasks waiting 40 s for a thread.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B platform backend (Java 21, 12 pods x 4 vCPU/8 GB, roughly $280 per pod per month, so about $3,400/month in total) uses one shared ThreadPoolExecutor(64, 64, queue 5000) named appPool for: customer-facing quote requests (p99 target 300 ms, avg task 40 ms of mostly DB wait), nightly-style CSV exports triggered by users (avg 20 s CPU+IO), and webhook deliveries to customers (avg 600 ms, p99 30 s because some endpoints are slow). Sales announces a 10x customer ramp over the quarter: 30 quotes/s per pod now -> 300/s; export requests from 0.2/s to 2/s per pod; webhooks 15/s to 150/s per pod. The CFO wants infra cost growth under 3x.
questions.promptHtml: Using numbers, how would you restructure the executors and what is the minimum scale-out you can justify?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale pods 10x" or "raise the pool to 640." Ignores workload isolation and the fact that the three workloads have very different resource profiles.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the DB/connection-pool limits? Are exports and webhooks latency-sensitive? Can exports run async in a job queue? Are webhook failures retried durably? What is peak vs average (burst factor)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Isolate first (it's cheap): split into three pools now, before the ramp, so exports and webhooks can no longer starve quotes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (where capacity goes today, per pod): Concurrency by Little's law L = rate x time. Quotes: 30 x 0.04 = 1.2 threads. Exports: 0.2 x 20 = 4 threads. Webhooks: 15 x 0.6 = 9 on average, but p99 30 s means the slow tail alone (say 5% of 15/s = 0.75/s x 30 s) = 22.5 threads. Total today ~37 average, spikes past 64. After 10x: quotes 12, exports 40, webhooks 90 average and ~225 for the slow tail = 360+ threads, so a single 64-thread pool would be crushed mostly by webhooks and exports, not quotes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-task-type timers and queue-wait metrics; JFR for CPU split; thread dump tags by task type; load test the 10x mix with k6.
  5. Root cause / insight: Capacity cost is dominated by slow, low-value work (webhook tails and exports), not the revenue-critical quotes. Scaling pods 10x to serve them in one pool buys idle capacity for quotes.
  6. Fix (design): Three bulkheaded pools: quotes sized for 12 average + headroom (say 32, bounded queue 50, abort -> 503); exports capped at 6 threads (CPU-bound, ~cores) with a durable job queue so extra exports wait (minutes are fine); webhooks moved off the pod to a queue-fed worker fleet with per-endpoint timeout (e.g. 5 s instead of 30 s), per-endpoint concurrency limits and circuit breakers, using virtual threads bounded by semaphores to carry the 150/s x 5 s = 750 concurrent waits cheaply. Quote path then scales with its own cost: 300/s per pod x 0.04 = 12 busy threads, DB connections are the limit, not CPU. Expected fleet: quotes can handle ~10x with maybe 3x pods (DB-bound; verify with a load test), exports in a separate 4-pod worker pool, webhooks in a small worker fleet; total cost growth plausibly ~3x rather than 10x.
ThreadPoolExecutor quotes = new ThreadPoolExecutor(32, 32, 0, SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(50), named("quotes"), new AbortPolicy());
ThreadPoolExecutor exports = new ThreadPoolExecutor(4, 6, 60, SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(20), named("exports"), new AbortPolicy());
Semaphore perEndpoint = new Semaphore(20); // webhook concurrency per customer endpoint
  1. Prevention: Per-pool dashboards and SLOs, capacity model in a doc re-run each quarter, fail tests when a task type lacks an owner pool, chaos test slow webhook endpoints.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More pools = more config and idle threads, offset by predictability. Moving webhooks off-pod adds an operational component. I would not mix virtual threads and unbounded fan-out without a semaphore, nor size to p99 tails for every pool when queueing and timeouts are acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The DB allows only 100 connections per pod; quotes need 12? → Fine, but exports and webhooks must not take connections from the same Hikari pool; give exports a small separate pool or read replica.
  • A big customer's webhook endpoint hangs? → Per-endpoint timeout, concurrency cap and circuit breaker; otherwise one customer consumes the worker fleet.
  • What if the CFO asks for 2x not 3x? → Cut webhook timeout further, batch/ coalesce deliveries, run exports off-peak on spot instances.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team doubled the fleet after an export feature slowed quotes. Splitting out exports to a small worker pool brought the fleet back down by 30% and fixed the p99 permanently.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scale linearly; one bigger pool.
  • Hire: Splits workloads into bulkheads, computes concurrency with Little's law.
  • Strong hire: Uses tail latency in the math, moves slow/low-value work off the serving fleet, aligns pools with DB limits, controls per-endpoint blast radius, and ties the plan to a measurable cost target.
